step: Follow one value inside an SM
title: Where does the multiplication happen?
text: In Chapter One, the GPU doubles five input values. Let’s follow one of them: one point zero becomes two point zero. The GPU program supplies instructions: individual operations such as a load, a multiply, or a store. A streaming multiprocessor, or S M, provides the hardware that performs those instructions. The input and output arrays are in GPU memory, outside the S M.

step: Load from memory into a register
title: Load the input.
lead: A register is small, fast storage inside the SM.
text: Thread Zero’s load requests the value at input index zero. Load and store units handle memory instructions. A load brings a value from memory into a register: a small, fast storage location inside the S M. Registers hold the working values that arithmetic instructions use. The request can take time; this diagram jumps ahead to when one point zero arrives in a register. The input array still holds its original value. Nothing has been written to the output array yet.

title: Multiply the register value.
lead: The result returns to a register. Output memory is still unwritten.
text: The multiply instruction uses the loaded value and the multiplier two. Floating point arithmetic units perform calculations on floating point values. Here, they produce two point zero and return the result to a register. Our values use thirty two bit floating point, often called F P thirty two. These arithmetic units are shared by threads, rather than permanently owned by Thread Zero. The multiply has not written the result to the output array. That needs a store.

step: Store the result in GPU memory
title: Write the result back.
text: The store is a separate instruction. Load and store units write two point zero from the thread’s result register into output index zero in GPU memory. The result is now in the output array. We have followed the whole value path: memory to register, arithmetic, then register to memory.

title: Another thread. Separate values.
lead: Thread 1 loads 2.0 while Thread 0’s values remain distinct.
text: Now inspect Thread One, whose input is two point zero. Its load supplies its own working register. Thread Zero’s values remain separate. We are changing which values we inspect, not choosing the GPU’s execution order. A GPU can execute instructions for groups of threads together; this picture isolates two threads to make their values easy to follow.

step: Reuse the same kinds of execution hardware
title: The hardware is shared.
text: Thread One’s multiply uses the same depicted floating point hardware, producing four point zero. Its store writes that result to output index one. Each thread has its own working values, while execution units are shared. The input and result columns identify values, not fixed physical registers. A register can be reused after a value is no longer needed. The boxes show hardware roles, not unit counts or exactly when instructions execute.

step: Pause and explain where the result is
title: Pause and explain.
lead: A third thread loads 3.0 and multiplies by 2. The store has not run.
question: Where is its result: a working register or the output array?
text: Try one more case. A third thread loads three point zero and multiplies it by two. Its store instruction has not run. Where is the result at this point: in a working register, or in the output array? Pause here and explain why.

step: Check the explanation and return to Chapter 1
title: Registers first. Memory after the store.
lead: The multiply produces 6.0 in a working register.
text: The result, six point zero, is in a working register. The store is what writes it to the output array. That is the distinction to take back to Chapter One: threads describe executions with separate working values. The S M provides shared hardware for loads, arithmetic and stores. This is a conceptual explanation, not a trace of the kernel PyTorch selected.
